opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting directions right now. The basic observation is that a lot of the progress in machine learning has come from replacing hand-designed components with learned ones, as long as you have enough compute to do the search. We did it with features, then with architectures to some extent. The question is: why stop at the model? Why not apply the same logic to the learning algorithm itself?

So when I talk about computation at the meta level, I mean spending compute not just on training one agent on one task, but on discovering the *process* that produces good agents across a whole distribution of tasks. That could be a learned optimizer, a learned objective function, or a learned update rule for reinforcement learning. If you meta-train over a broad enough distribution, what you get is an algorithm that has absorbed regularities about learning itself, rather than about any one environment. And that's exactly what you want for generalization: when you drop it into a new situation, it's not relying on memorized solutions, it's relying on a learned way of adapting.

The catch, historically, has been that this is ridiculously expensive. You have an inner loop that's a full training run, and an outer loop on top. That's where hardware acceleration and things like JAX have been a game changer for us. If you can run the environment and the agent end to end on the accelerator, vectorize across thousands of environments, you suddenly get orders of magnitude speedups. Experiments that used to need a cluster for weeks you can do on a few GPUs in hours. That changes what questions you can even ask.

The other piece, which I think matters just as much, is the distribution of tasks you meta-train on. If you only meta-learn on a narrow set of environments, you'll get something that overfits at the meta level. So we've been very interested in open-endedness and automatic curriculum design: having the system generate its own environments, pushing toward the frontier of what the agent can just barely solve. In a sense, compute goes into generating the problems as well as the solutions.

And I'd add one caution: generalization at the meta level isn't free. You have to be really careful about evaluation, actually holding out genuinely different tasks, otherwise it's very easy to fool yourself. But in principle, I think scaling compute at the meta level is one of the more promising paths toward agents that can handle situations nobody designed them for.

r001.rationale: The response proposes spending compute to discover learning processes, such as learned optimizers and update rules, but does not say these algorithms should be sample-efficient.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss humans, few-sample learning, or evolution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about this is that generalization is fundamentally about where you spend your compute. If you spend all of your compute at the object level, training a single policy on a single environment, you get a system that's very good at exactly that environment and tends to fall over the moment the distribution shifts. And I think a lot of the brittleness we see in deep RL comes from exactly that.

What meta-level computation lets you do is step back and ask a different question. Instead of "what's the best policy for this problem," you ask "what's the best learning process, or the best objective, or the best environment distribution, such that whatever comes out the other end is robust to problems I haven't seen yet." So you're optimizing over the thing that produces the solution, rather than the solution itself. And once you do that, you can score candidates on generalization directly, because you can hold out tasks, hold out opponents, hold out dynamics, and the outer loop actually gets a gradient toward being adaptable rather than toward memorizing.

A nice example from our own work is unsupervised environment design. There, the meta level is a curriculum: an adversary or a regret-based mechanism that picks which environments the agent should be trained on next. The agent at the object level is still just doing standard RL, but the system as a whole is searching over the training distribution, and what pops out is an agent that transfers to levels nobody ever hand-designed. The same philosophy shows up when you meta-learn the objective function itself. We've had cases where a learned RL loss discovered on tiny toy problems ends up working on Atari, which tells you the meta level found something more like a general principle of learning rather than a trick for one setting.

There's also a multi-agent angle that I care about a lot. In things like Hanabi, or any setting where you need to coordinate with a partner you've never met, the failure mode of naive self-play is that you learn arbitrary conventions that only work with yourself. The fix is again meta-level: you reason about the space of possible partners, or you introduce symmetries and constraints into the learning process so that the policy you produce is one that a different, independently trained agent could also plausibly arrive at. That's compute at the meta level buying you generalization across agents rather than across environments.

Now, the honest caveat is that meta-level optimization is expensive, and you can easily just push the overfitting up one level. If your meta-training distribution is narrow, you get a learning algorithm that's brilliant on that distribution and useless elsewhere. So the design of the outer loop, what you vary and what you hold out, is doing a lot of the work. But I think that's actually the right place to be spending human effort. Rather than hand-crafting the agent, we should be hand-crafting the pressures that force the agent to become general, and then letting compute do the rest. In the long run I'd expect most of the interesting structure in these systems to come from that outer loop rather than from anything we wrote down directly.

r001.rationale: The response describes using meta-level computation to optimize learning processes and objectives, but does not clearly propose large-scale computation to discover sample-efficient learning algorithms.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss humans’ ability to learn from few samples or attribute it to an evolutionarily produced, sample-inefficient process.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting possibility is to use computation to learn how to learn, rather than just to learn a fixed solution. You can spend a lot of computation during training exposing a system to different situations, and ask it to discover an update rule or a strategy for adapting. Then, when it encounters a new situation, it has a useful way of learning from the information available there.

But that doesn’t make the generalization problem disappear. You still have to ask: what structure do the training situations share with the new one? If you meta-train over a narrow set of tasks, you can overfit at the meta level just as you can at the object level.

So the promise, to me, is that we can use computation to discover learning procedures that we would otherwise have to design by hand. The crucial question is whether those procedures capture something reusable, rather than simply exploiting regularities in the particular tasks we gave them.

r001.rationale: It proposes using computation to discover learning procedures, but does not say they should be sample-efficient or characterize the computation as large-scale.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss humans, few-sample learning, or evolution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is where you spend the computation. You can spend it learning a particular solution, but you can also spend it learning a procedure that finds solutions. At the meta level, you’re asking: what should the learning algorithm itself look like, so that when it encounters a new situation, it can adapt efficiently?

For example, rather than training an agent to succeed in one fixed environment, you could train it across a family of environments where it has to discover something about each one. Now there’s an incentive to learn how to explore, which information to retain, and how to use that information to change its behavior.

But there’s a caveat: you haven’t made the generalization problem disappear. You’ve moved it up a level. If all your training environments share some shortcut, your learned learning algorithm can exploit that shortcut too. So the promise is that computation can help us discover more general adaptation mechanisms. Whether those mechanisms actually generalize depends on the diversity and structure of the problems we use to discover them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using computation to discover adaptation mechanisms and says agents can adapt efficiently, but it does not clearly propose large-scale computation to discover sample-efficient learning algorithms.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention humans, few-sample learning, or evolution as the source of that ability.
